extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, policy analysts, researchers and graduate students studying media economics, journalism, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and measurable criteria for studying how market forces, regulation, and technology shape news content across outlets and countries; includes methods for content analysis, search-patterns, surveys, and policy evaluation. Geared toward empirical research and policy assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rights to create and disseminate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in property rights and legal/regulatory constraints (state control, defamation laws, licensing, required local partners for global firms, Internet filters, election/campaign finance laws) affect what outlets choose to cover and their incentives to self-censor or pursue soft vs hard news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether government ownership, licensing regimes, libel/defamation rules, or requirements for local partners create incentives for outlets to avoid controversial coverage. Examples: private outlets focusing on soft news to avoid censorship; local partners steering content to appease government; Internet café filters or cybercensorship blocking political content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product differentiation (analytical lens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat news outlets as differentiated products located along multiple dimensions (hard/soft mix, political orientation, language/style, reliance on personalities). Quantify product-location decisions to test theories of how competition changes content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-sectional snapshots of outlets to compare product positions; combine content measures, audience metrics, and surveys. Product differentiation is an umbrella for several measurable dimensions (see separate entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard/soft news mix
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which an outlet focuses on hard public affairs news (policy, legislative votes, court decisions) versus soft news (celebrity, lifestyle, entertainment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure by counting number of stories or time devoted to policy events versus celebrity/human-interest pieces; use specific hard-news markers (e.g., coverage of key Congressional votes, Supreme Court cases) and soft-news exemplars (e.g., People magazine features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political orientation of the news outlet
rubrics_metrics.description: The outlet's location on the left–right political spectrum, which can be operationalized by the issues, frames, language, sources cited, or party-affiliated stances adopted in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map outlet positions by comparing coverage to party platforms, analyzing which think tanks or sources are cited, and coding use of partisan adjectives (e.g., 'liberal'/'conservative', 'right-wing'/'left-wing'). Use content analysis to see whether outlets preferentially adopt particular frames or labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language use (textual indicators / DICTION)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure differences in word use and textual features across outlets (frequency of personal pronouns, human-interest words, collectives, complexity, variety). The DICTION software example: 500-word samples compared with ~10,000 terms divided into 33 lists producing 40 indicators and five summary measures (certainty, optimism, activity, realism, commonality) plus complexity and variety counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run sampled articles/transcripts through text-analysis tools (e.g., DICTION) to obtain relative frequencies for the 33 word lists and the 40 indicators, use the five summary measures and complexity/variety metrics to compare outlets. For non-English texts, use equivalent word-frequency programs or translated dictionaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal presentation choices that affect audience appeal: article length, sentence complexity, use of visuals, rapid delivery, number of shots/video clips, on-screen information, and mixing politics with personal storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify features from print/broadcast samples (e.g., average article length, average sentence complexity, number of images/graphics, shot length, frequency of on-screen banners). Some features require manual coding of broadcasts (e.g., rapid delivery, camera use, narrative framing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on news personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which an outlet foregrounds anchors/hosts/reporters/columnists as part of the product identity (camera time, promoted columnists, smaller roster of recognizable reporters with higher pay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure camera/column inches devoted to named personalities, frequency of anchor commentary, staffing patterns (fewer but promoted reporters), and salary/promotion evidence. Interpret increased personality dependence as product differentiation strategy in competitive markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information search patterns (demand-side measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of search engine query data, lists of most-emailed or most-viewed stories, and story rankings to infer audience interests and demand for particular topics in Internet markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect search-frequency data (e.g., Google trends), most-emailed/viewed lists from news sites, and proprietary surfing patterns where available; use these topics as inputs for content analysis and to estimate relative audience demand for types of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring censorship and blocked information via Internet tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess what information searches and sites are blocked/filtered in a country and whether posted controversial comments are deleted, to gauge government-imposed or de facto censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform searches from within country, record blocked sites, post controversial comments and monitor moderation/removal, and compare blocked/censored Internet content to what official and commercial newspapers publish to identify topics reserved for government or avoided by private media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumption surveys and audience measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use audience survey data (e.g., Nielsen), public opinion polls on media consumption, and demographic ad analysis to determine who consumes particular programs/outlets and how outlets are perceived (e.g., political bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze program-level audience demographics, poll respondents' perceptions of outlet bias, and cross-tabulate knowledge or information levels among audiences. Note limitations: sample sizes vary, access to proprietary data is limited, and survey instruments must be designed to capture perceptions accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production surveys of journalists (supply-side insight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey journalists about the impact of economic and political factors on content decisions to complement inferences from audience and content data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design anonymous surveys to mitigate fear of reprisal (in repressive contexts). Recognize limits: journalists may underreport market influences, fear government reprisal, or lack full visibility into managerial incentives; treat survey responses as one piece of evidence alongside content/ad/audience data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using advertising content to infer target demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze ads in newspapers and TV programs to deduce the targeted demographic for a media outlet and thus infer incentives shaping content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code ad categories, advertised products, and audience-targeted messaging to map advertiser preferences; combine ad analysis with audience demographics and content to triangulate outlet incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory environment and ownership structures as determinants of content
rubrics_metrics.description: Country-specific institutional features (degree of press freedom, state ownership, press club systems, libel rulings, foreign joint-venture requirements, local partners) shape incentives for self-censorship, investigative reporting, and the balance between entertainment and public-affairs coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cross-country comparisons, document ownership patterns, legal constraints (e.g., defamation fines), licensing regimes, and institutional practices (e.g., press clubs) and relate them to observed content mixes and instances of self-censorship or selective investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of information technology and citizen journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: New technologies (cellphone text messaging, blogs, citizen journalism sites) can alter news circulation, mobilization, and the balance between professional and volunteer reporting, affecting market incentives and political outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure penetration/usage of mobile and Internet platforms, track volume and uptake of citizen-generated content (e.g., submissions and publication rates on sites like OhMyNews), and analyze case studies where technology-enabled information flows influenced events (e.g., protest mobilization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasible (policy assessment criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a proposed policy to change media content is realistically implementable given economic and political obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal, fiscal, administrative, and political barriers to adoption; consider institutional capacity and enforcement feasibility when evaluating policy proposals (e.g., non-profit ownership incentives, subsidies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operable (policy assessment criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: How likely a policy is to induce actual changes in hard-news production and whether those content changes will translate into changes in consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the mechanisms by which the policy affects reporters' and owners' incentives, predict the content changes expected, and consider whether audience behavior will respond; look for intermediate indicators (e.g., story counts, staffing changes) to validate operability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desirable (policy assessment criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the ultimate impacts of a policy on voter knowledge, political debate, and policy outcomes are positive and how implementation might go wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential unintended consequences (e.g., capture by partisan actors, distortion of coverage), distributional effects, and normative goals; link content changes to plausible effects on civic knowledge and democratic deliberation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurable (policy assessment criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the effects of a proposed policy can be assessed using observable indicators and how one would know if the policy is working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define concrete metrics (e.g., counts of hard-news stories, audience knowledge measures, changes in investigative reporting frequency, audience demographics), set baseline measurements, and specify data sources and evaluation timelines to judge success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for positive externalities and choosing corrective tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that news production/consumption involves positive externalities (public benefits not private), and that policy tools (taxes, subsidies, regulation, government provision, property-rights definitions) can be used to try to internalize these externalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing interventions, specify which tool addresses which market failure, be explicit about assumptions (about behavioral responses and probabilities), and plan for imperfect indicators and disagreement among analysts; use cost–benefit style questions (feasible, operable, desirable, measurable) to structure evaluation.
